newsitem.title: USA: Fed policy-makers unanimously backed March rate rise.
newsitem.headline: Fed policy-makers unanimously backed March rate rise.

text.p: Federal Reserve policy-makers decided unanimously in March to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point, although a few would have preferred a bigger increase, minutes of their meeting showed.

The minutes, released Thursday with the customary six-week lag, painted a picture of a central bank increasingly worried about the risk of faster inflation but divided over how big a danger that posed to the economy.

At its most recent policy-making meeting on Tuesday, the central bank's Federal Open Market Committee left interest rates unchanged, apparently in hopes that the economy will slow from its recent break-neck pace. Minutes of that meeting will not be released until July 3.
At their March 25 meeting, Fed policy-makers saw an economic slowdown as inevitable, but were uncertain about its timing and its magnitude, according to the minutes.

In their forecast prepared for the March meeting, Fed staff predicted that growth would slow in coming quarters to a pace "somewhat above that of the economy's estimated potential" before moderating a bit more in 1998.

The economy expanded at a 5.6 percent annualized pace in the first quarter, its fastest clip in more than nine years and well above the 2.0 to 2.5 percent rate considered sustainable in the long-run without fanning inflation.
According to the minutes of the March 25 meeting, all the FOMC members saw a clear need for a preemptive interest rate increase to head off any pickup in inflation.
They also agreed that the higher rates would pose little risk to the economic expansion and instead would help sustain it by keeping price rises in check.

The Fed tightened credit in March for the first time in more than two years, bumping up the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent.
"A few members argued that a more substantial tightening was needed," the minutes said. "In their view, a more vigorous action would lessen the need for tightening in the future."
However, other members urged a more cautious approach, given the uncertain outlook for the economy and inflation.

The central bank panel was also divided initially over what stance to take in the approach to this week's meeting. Some wanted to adopt a policy that was biased toward raising rates further. A majority did not, although they admitted that some further tightening of credit might be needed eventually.
In the end, the FOMC unanimously adopted a neutral stance that presumed neither higher nor lower interest rates during the period leading up to this week's meeting.
In deciding to raise rates on March 25, the FOMC recognised that what it called "inflationary developments" had become a more urgent concern.
"The risks now seemed to be tilted more clearly toward higher inflation," the FOMC minutes said.
Temporary factors that had helped hold down labour costs -- such as worker fears about job loss -- seemed about to wane, and might already have begun doing so, the minutes said.
Nevertheless, the FOMC members acknowledged that inflation had remained "remarkably subdued" and that any increase in inflationary pressures was likely to occur only slowly.
